title: Force between two parallel current-carrying conductors
topicTitle: Force between two parallel current-carrying conductors
notes: A long straight wire produces circles of magnetic field. A second wire, parallel to the first, carries current across that field and feels a force F = I L B sinθ. With the wires parallel, θ is 90°.
Substituting B = μ0 I1 /(2π r) gives the force per unit length F/L = μ0 I1 I2 /(2π r). The force is mutual: each wire feels the same magnitude.
If the currents are in the same direction the force is attractive. If they are in opposite directions the force is repulsive. The right-hand rule on one wire's field, then on the force, gives this.
The ampere was historically defined from this force: two long parallel wires, 1 m apart, carrying 1 A each, attract with 2 × 10^−7 N per metre of length.

The wires must be long compared with their separation, or the formula is only a middle-region estimate. The field is not uniform, but the result above is already the integrated force on a straight parallel wire.
Coils and bus bars use the same idea. Parallel turns of a solenoid attract. A short-circuit current in opposite bus bars pushes them apart.

keyPoints: • Force between two parallel current-carrying conductors
Each wire sits in the other's field.
Parallel currents in the same direction attract.
The force per unit length is the definition behind the ampere.
summary: Parallel wires feel F/L = μ0 I1 I2 /(2π r) because each sits in the other's field. Currents in the same direction attract and opposite currents repel. The old definition of the ampere is this force at 1 m separation.
